Case Report 
The patient. a 6-year-old boy, was admitted to the hospital 
because of stiffness in both legs, internal rotation of the feet, 
and painful muscle spasms in the lower extremities with diffi- 
culty in walking. These symptoms started 24 hours before ad- 
mission. The stiffness spread upward over 5 days, involving the 
trunk. 
The patient had no siblings and there was no familial history 
of neurologic disease. He had an unremarkable past medical 
history and was properly vaccinated, including tetanus immu- 
nization. No history of recent injury, exposure to toxic sub- 
stances, febrile or systemic illness was obtained. 
On neurologic examination, intellect and cranial nerves were 
normal. Muscle tone and strength in the arms were also normal. 
Both legs were rigid with marked knee hyperextension and 
sustained equinus position of the feet. There was a persistent 
contraction of axial muscles, especially abdominal and lumbar 
paraspinal muscles, causing a permanent hyperlordosis of the 
lumbar spine. Certain movements such as walking, sitting from 
a lying position, or rolling on the bed were impaired as a result 
of the rigid posture of the legs and trunk, giving the patient the 
appearance of a “wooden man.” 
Superimposed on this persistent stiffness, there were fre- 
quent painful muscle spasms lasting from seconds to several 
minutes. These spasms were spontaneous and were also pre- 
cipitated by different stimuli such as light touching, unexpected 
noises (telephone ring), or passive leg movements. Muscle 
spasms were so severe that they frequently rendered the patient 
in a distressing posture of opisthotonus. 
The axial stiffness and muscle spasms still persisted, al- 
though with reduced intensity, during the initial stages of sleep, 
The remainder of the neurologic examination, including sen- 
sation, tendon reflexes, and plantar responses, was normal. 
General physical examination was unremarkable. 
Electromyographic recordings from lumbar paraspinal 
muscles, quadnceps, and tibialis anterior showed continuous 
motor unit activity at rest frequently reaching an interference 
pattern, with superimposed muscles spasms, which were either 
spontaneous or induced by different exteroceptive stimuli (Fig. 
1). The motor unit potentials were normal and no spontaneous

The electrical stimulation of mixed nerves and cutaneous 
areas of the lower extremity induced the appearance of late 
motor responses following the direct evoked motor potential, 
showing several consistent bursts of electromyographic activity 
at regular intervals. This late reflex activity was also found in 
muscles not related to the stimulated nerve or skin area and 
even in muscles of the contralateral limb (Fig. 2). The silent 
period obtained on a muscular spasm after a supramaximal 
electrical stimulation of the peroneal nerve was preserved. 
Routine hematologic tests and blood biochemistry, including 
glucose, Ca, P, Na, K, Mg, creatine kinase, liver function tests, 
lactate, pyruvate, carnitine, copper, and ceruloplasmin, were 
normal. Amino acids and organic acids were normal in serum 
and urine. Routine cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was also normal 
and no oligoclonal IgG bands were found. Immunoglobulins 
were normal in both serum and CSF. Serologic investigations 
for viral agents were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord did 
not disclose any abnormality. The patient was treated with a 
combination of oral diazepam (up to 
22 mg/day) and baclofen 
(up to 15 mg/day) with a marked improvement of the axial 
stiffness and almost complete abolition of the muscle spasms. 
Nine months later, the patient's clinical situation remained 
unchanged.

This case fulfilled the proposed criteria for the clinical di- 
agnosis of SMS,',""' except for the acute onset of the symp- 
toms. The initial rapid progression of rigidity and muscle 
spasms involving the legs and trunk led us to consider other 
possible entities such as progressive encephalomyelitis with 
rigidity." However, the absence of cranial nerve involvement, 
the presence of normal tendon jerks, and the lack of abnormal 
findings in the CSF and MRI of the brain and spinal cord, along 
with a good response to the treatment with diazepam and bac- 
lofen, made that diagnosis unlikely. Furthermore, some adult-

Nevertheless, an overlap between SMS and progressive en- 
cephalomyelitis with rigidity has been suggested. 
The pathophysiology of SMS remains unclear. An abnormal 
excitability of spinal interneuronal pathways has been sug- 
ge~ted.~.'~ In our case, the electrophysiological findings, espe- 
cially the late motor responses evoked by electrical stimulation 
of a motor nerve of the lower extremity and its spreading to the 
contralateral limb, are in agreement with this hypothesis. A 
similar pattern of late EMG bursts in the trunk muscles induced 
by median nerve stimulation have also been reported in adult- 
onset SMS.16 
Solimena et al. described autoantibodies directed against 
gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic neurons, specifically 
reacting with GAD by Western blot and immunoprecipitation 
assays, in 60% of patients with SMS who had in addition other 
organ-specific autoantibodies or autoimmune diseases." These 
findings point to an autoimmune origin of the SMS, suggesting 
a possible autoimmune attack to GABA-ergic neurons, and 
give additional support to the hypothesis of dysfunction of the 
spinal inhibitory networks mediated by GABA, along with the 
clinical improvement obtained with GABA-ergic drugs such as 
clonazepam and baclofen. However, SMS appears to be a het- 
erogeneous immunologic disorder because other autoantibodies 
have been found in SMS of likely autoimmune paraneoplastic 
orjginl".20 and nearly 40% of clinically diagnosed SMS do not 
show any known autoantibody. Our patient may be included in 
the latter group of SMS. 
This case confirms that SMS can occur in childhood. It may 
differ from the usual adult SMS in having a more acute onset 
and the absence of anti-GAD autoantibodies.
